prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the one candidate on the table where the origin is sharp, the performance gain is quantified, and independent confirmation is complete. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removed the trade-off between Doppler and recoil-free confinement and the light shift of the lattice, and Ye's group then drove accuracy and stability to the 1e-18 level and used many-body (spin-polarised Fermi gas) lattice clocks to expose and control systematics. Several laboratories on different continents now agree below 1e-18 and compare clocks routinely, which is the kind of reproducibility a prize should rest on. The consequences are concrete: millimetre-scale tests of gravitational redshift and relativistic geodesy, tighter limits on drifts of fundamental constants, searches for ultralight dark matter, and the live international discussion on redefining the second. Six of the eight members ranked it in their top three, and all six proposed the same two names. Because I work in atomic structure and precision calculations, I can judge that the underlying physics, including the control of blackbody-radiation and other level shifts, is soundly understood rather than merely demonstrated once.
statement.case_against: The strongest counterarguments are that this is an invention and technique with an extraordinary metrology payoff but a modest conceptual reorganisation of physics compared with, for example, topological or moire matter, and that it follows the 2005 prize for the frequency comb and precision spectroscopy and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems, so the committee may feel the atomic-clock territory has been recognised. A two-name prize also omits other lattice-clock pioneers (for instance the Paris and NIST groups) and the trapped-ion clock community, and it leaves the prospective redefinition of the second not yet completed, so one could argue the culminating step is still ahead.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first as a genuine new window on the universe, a discovery in nature, and ranks the lattice clock third as a clear and important invention that overlaps earlier precision-spectroscopy prizes.
responses.response: I accept that IceCube is the stronger candidate on the discovery-in-nature criterion and I ranked it low mainly because of my lack of expertise and the diffuse attribution, not because the neutrino flux is in doubt. Where I disagree is the overlap argument. The 2005 prize recognised the comb and comb-based spectroscopy; the lattice clock is a separate invention, resting on the magic-wavelength condition, that changed what the best clocks are and is not a refinement of the comb. On attribution I note he reduced the credit to Halzen and Karle while I kept Yoshida; I do not think the credit among the three is settled, and that makes a three-person IceCube prize the harder one to defend.

responses.point: Olsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, valuing the prediction followed by decisive experiments, the tunable platform and the wide reproduction, while noting the interpretation of the correlated phases is still evolving.
responses.response: I share her view of the originality and I ranked it third. My reservation is maturity, as she partly says herself: the existence of the flat-band-related insulators is solid, but the origin of the superconductivity and the sample dependence remain open, and the experimental credit leaves out first authors and other groups (Cao, Fatemi, and the hBN moire work) in a way that a three-name prize cannot repair. I would not oppose it as a prize in a year or two, but I do not see the case for placing it above a result that is already fully settled.

responses.point: Johansson ranks topological insulators first as a new class of quantum matter, timely and arguably overdue, and credits Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan rather than Mele.
responses.response: I agree that the physics is of the highest originality and that it is mature, and I ranked it fourth with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. I disagree with dropping Mele: the Kane-Mele Z2 formulation is the decisive theoretical step and I find it hard to credit Kane alone for it. More generally the topological-insulator credit has several competing claimants (Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, Fu, Hasan) and the 2016 prize already covered topological phases, so I think the attribution problem here is larger than in the clock case, where he and I both see a clean two-person credit.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first and the lattice clock second, regarding the attribution as clean (Katori the concept, Ye the performance) and noting that the redefinition of the second has not yet occurred.
responses.response: We agree on the clock credit and on its maturity, and I think his observation that the redefinition of the second is still ahead cuts in favour of prize timing rather than against it: the evidence base is already sufficient. On IceCube I part from him on how well three names can represent a large collaboration; he leaves Yoshida out, and I think that shows how arbitrary any cut is. If the committee prefers the neutrino discovery I could support it as a strong alternative, but I would want a clearer account of the individual contributions first.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as a sufficiently distinct achievement from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes.
Whether two names fairly represent lattice-clock priority given the early Paris and NIST contributions, which I cannot weigh from the supplied credit alone.
The relative weight of an invention with metrological payoff against discoveries in nature such as IceCube, which the opening ballots do not settle.
Whether the unresolved superconductivity mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene will be settled soon enough to change its standing.
statement.conflict_note: I have no documented personal or institutional connection to Katori or Ye, to Cirac or Zoller, or to the twisted-graphene candidates in the provided profile. I do work in theoretical atomic physics and collaborate with Anne L'Huillier's Lund group and Ursula Keller's group at ETH, so I am professionally close to the atomic, molecular and optical community and would flag any shortlisted AMO candidate that involves those groups; none is apparent among the credited names here.
